Martin-Löf test of unidimensionality

Source: R/martin_lof.R
RMdimMartinLof.Rd

Likelihood-ratio test of unidimensionality against a multidimensional alternative specified in advance, for Rasch and partial credit models (Christensen, Bjorner, Kreiner, & Petersen, 2002). The p-value comes from a parametric bootstrap under the unidimensional model, following Christensen and Kreiner (2007), since the asymptotic chi-square distribution makes the test conservative at realistic sample sizes, especially with polytomous items, where the degrees of freedom can be very large.

Usage

RMdimMartinLof(
  data,
  partition,
  iterations = 1000L,
  stopping = c("none", "sequential"),
  h = 50L,
  alpha = 0.05,
  parallel = TRUE,
  n_cores = NULL,
  verbose = FALSE,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data.frame or matrix of item responses, items scored from 0. Only complete cases on the items in partition are used. Missing values on other items are ignored.

partition

The hypothesised partition of the items into subscales. Either:

  • a list of column-name or column-index vectors, for example list(c("I1","I2","I3"), c("I4","I5","I6")), or

  • a vector of length ncol(data) giving each item's subscale (factor, character or integer), for example c(1,1,1,2,2,2).

Each subscale must have at least two items, and subscales must not overlap. Items not in any subscale are dropped with a warning.

iterations

Integer. Largest number of simulated datasets. Default 1000.

stopping

Character. "none" (default) runs all iterations. "sequential" uses the sequential rule of Besag and Clifford (1991), stopping as soon as h simulated statistics have exceeded the observed one. This saves much time when the unidimensional model holds, but it cannot run in parallel.

h

Integer. The count for sequential stopping. Default 50. Ignored with stopping = "none".

alpha

Numeric in (0, 1). Used only for the rejected element of the result. Default 0.05.

parallel

Logical. Run the simulations in parallel via mirai when it is installed. Default TRUE. Ignored with stopping = "sequential".

n_cores

Integer or NULL. Number of parallel workers. When NULL, getOption("mc.cores") is used. If that is unset too, a warning is given and the simulations run sequentially.

verbose

Logical. Show a progress bar. Default FALSE.

seed

Integer or NULL. Random seed for reproducibility. Items are processed in a fixed (alphabetical) order, so the same seed gives the same p-value whatever the order of the columns and the parallel setting. See easyRasch2-reproducibility for what this guarantees and how it interacts with parallel.

Value

A list with components:

T_obs

Observed Martin-Löf likelihood-ratio statistic.

p_value

Monte Carlo p-value, (n_exceed + 1) / (n + 1) for n simulated datasets. The possible values are k / (n + 1) for k = 1, ..., n + 1, so the number of iterations limits the resolution. With 100 iterations the smallest possible value is 1/101 = 0.0099. A p-value equal to the floor (p_value_floor) means no simulated statistic reached the observed one. Read it as "p < floor", since the true p-value may be much smaller, and increase iterations for finer resolution.

p_value_floor

The smallest attainable p-value, 1 / (actual_iterations + 1).

actual_iterations

Number of simulated datasets used.

requested_iterations

The iterations requested.

failed_iterations

Number of simulated datasets that could not be refitted and were left out. With stopping = "sequential", actual_iterations can also be below requested_iterations because the rule stopped early.

rejected

Logical: is p_value < alpha?

partition

Normalised partition (list of integer indices).

n_subscales

Number of subscales.

is_polytomous

Whether a PCM was fitted.

sample_n

Number of complete cases analysed, counted over the items in partition only.

sample_n_total

Number of respondents in the raw input data, before the complete-case filter.

sample_has_na

Logical. Whether the partitioned items contained any missing values.

n_items

Number of items.

stopping

The stopping strategy used.

h

The sequential-stopping count, or NA for stopping = "none".

T_rep

The simulated test statistics.

wle_scores

data.frame with one row per person and one column per subscale (subscale_1_wle, ..., subscale_D_wle), giving Warm's weighted likelihood estimate of theta from a CML fit on each subscale alone. Persons with the lowest or highest possible subscore on a subscale get non-finite WLEs (Inf or -Inf) and are left out of wle_correlation pairwise.

wle_correlation

data.frame of pairwise Pearson correlations between subscale WLEs, with columns subscale_a, subscale_b, r, ci_lower, ci_upper (95% CI from stats::cor.test), p_value, and n (number of persons with finite WLEs on both subscales). One row per pair, so a single row for D = 2. Useful as an effect size next to p_value. A rejected test with r near 1 indicates a small departure, and r clearly below 1 substantial multidimensionality.

Details

This is not a screening tool. The partition of items into subscales must be decided in advance. Testing a partition suggested by the data, such as the signs of the first-component loadings in RMdimResidualPCA(), would inflate the type I error rate. Both source papers say so.

Test statistic. With items partitioned into D subscales, total score \(t\) and subscores \((t_1, \ldots, t_D)\) (Christensen et al. 2002, eq. 22): $$T = 2\Bigl[\sum_{t_1, \ldots, t_D} n_{t_1, \ldots, t_D}\log(n_{t_1, \ldots, t_D}/N) - \sum_t n_t\log(n_t/N) - \ell_C(\hat{\epsilon}) + \sum_d \ell_C(\hat{\epsilon}^{(d)})\Bigr]$$ where \(\ell_C\) is the conditional log-likelihood and the \(\hat{\epsilon}^{(d)}\) are CML estimates on the d-th subscale alone. CML fits use psychotools::raschmodel() (RM) or psychotools::pcmodel() (PCM) for speed.

Monte Carlo sampling under H0. Following Christensen & Kreiner (2007): (a) sample N total scores from the empirical score distribution \(n_t/N\), and (b) for each sampled score, sample an item-response vector from the conditional distribution \(p(x \mid t, \hat{\epsilon})\) given by eq. 4 of the paper. Step (b) uses the recursive \(\gamma\)-function algorithm (Andersen, 1995, eq. 15.22 and 15.27) for dichotomous and polytomous items alike: items are filled in from the last backwards, each conditional on the score still to be distributed over the items before it. The nested \(\gamma^{(1)}, \ldots, \gamma^{(n)}\) depend only on the item parameters, which are fixed across the run, so the recursion is evaluated once rather than per person.

The faster dichotomous shortcut described by Christensen & Kreiner (2007, p. 23), choosing \(s\) items one at a time with probabilities \(\phi_i / \sum_{\mathrm{remaining}} \phi\), is deliberately not used: successive sampling of that kind follows a Wallenius-type distribution, whereas the Rasch conditional distribution weights a set of items by the product of their easinesses. See the note on validation below.

A simulated dataset that cannot be refitted, for example because a category of an item is empty, is left out, with a message saying how many. actual_iterations gives the number used and failed_iterations the number left out.

Item parameters are estimated once on the observed data and held fixed across MC iterations. Christensen & Kreiner (2007) use the extended likelihood function (Tjur, 1982) with the empirical score distribution as a non-parametric estimate of the latent distribution, so no distributional assumption about \(\theta\) is needed.

Missing data. Complete cases only. The statistic is built from the joint table of subscores, so a respondent needs a subscore on every subscale. The SAS macro this implementation was validated against has the same requirement. Rows with NA are dropped after items outside partition have been removed, so missingness on items the test does not use costs no respondents. sample_n reports the respondents analysed and sample_n_total the raw input rows.

Validation. The statistic, the conditional log-likelihoods, the conditional sampler and the expected counts and residuals of RMdimMartinLofResiduals have been checked against the pml SAS macro (Christensen, 2004), kindly shared by Karl Bang Christensen. The statistic and the residual table agree with the macro to numerical precision. The sampler follows the macro's recursion rather than the dichotomous shortcut published in Christensen & Kreiner (2007).

References

Andersen, E. B. (1995). Polytomous Rasch models and their estimation. In G. H. Fischer & I. W. Molenaar (Eds.), Rasch models: Foundations, recent developments, and applications (pp. 271-291). Springer-Verlag.

Besag, J., & Clifford, P. (1991). Sequential Monte Carlo p-values. Biometrika, 78(2), 301-304. doi:10.1093/biomet/78.2.301

Christensen, K. B. (2004). pml: A SAS macro for testing unidimensionality in polytomous Rasch models (Technical note). National Institute of Occupational Health, Denmark, and Department of Biostatistics, University of Copenhagen.

Christensen, K. B., Bjorner, J. B., Kreiner, S., & Petersen, J. H. (2002). Testing unidimensionality in polytomous Rasch models. Psychometrika, 67(4), 563-574. doi:10.1007/BF02295131

Christensen, K. B., & Kreiner, S. (2007). A Monte Carlo approach to unidimensionality testing in polytomous Rasch models. Applied Psychological Measurement, 31(1), 20-30. doi:10.1177/0146621605286204

Tjur, T. (1982). A connection between Rasch's item analysis model and a multiplicative Poisson model. Scandinavian Journal of Statistics, 9(1), 23-30.

See also

RMdimMartinLofResiduals() for where the partition departs, RMdimResidualPCA() and RMdimCFA() for other checks of unidimensionality.

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
# Two-dimensional partial credit data: 4 items per subscale, 5 categories,
# latent correlation 0.6
n <- 400
theta1 <- rnorm(n)
theta2 <- 0.6 * theta1 + sqrt(1 - 0.6^2) * rnorm(n)
sim_pcm <- function(theta, n_items) {
  sapply(seq_len(n_items), function(j) {
    thr <- c(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5) + (j - 2.5) * 0.3
    lp <- outer(theta, 0:4) - matrix(c(0, cumsum(thr)), length(theta), 5,
                                     byrow = TRUE)
    p <- exp(lp) / rowSums(exp(lp))
    apply(p, 1, function(pr) sample(0:4, 1, prob = pr))
  })
}
dat <- cbind(sim_pcm(theta1, 4), sim_pcm(theta2, 4))
colnames(dat) <- paste0("I", 1:8)

# Few iterations for a fast example. Use 1000 or more in real analyses.
RMdimMartinLof(dat,
            partition = list(c("I1","I2","I3","I4"),
                             c("I5","I6","I7","I8")),
            iterations = 100, parallel = FALSE, seed = 1)

# Sequential stopping: stop as soon as h = 25 simulated statistics exceed
# the observed one (cuts compute time under H0).
RMdimMartinLof(dat,
            partition = c(1,1,1,1,2,2,2,2),
            iterations = 200, stopping = "sequential", h = 25,
            seed = 1)
